transcript:
Meeting Header: 2027-05-11 15:30 UTC | Duration ~75m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Aurelia ML), Marco Ruiz (Aurelia Infra), Dalia Wong (Aurelia SRE), Tom Becker (Aurelia Product)

Summary:
- Deep technical triage of recent accuracy regressions after mixed-precision deployment (int8 / AWQ / FP8 variants).
- Focus areas: layerwise sensitivity, KV cache warmup/staleness, batching/coalescing side effects, and onprem VPC network noise.
- Agreed next steps: repro on customer prompts, run deterministic GPTQ vs stochastic AWQ comparison, schedule onprem profiling.

Topics:
- Root-cause hypotheses (quantization-induced activation distribution shift, layerwise rounding drift, KV cache stale states).
- Warmup and cache priming strategies to reduce transient degradation.
- Tradeoffs: latency vs regen quality across int8/gptq/awq/fp8.
- Canary strategies and rollback for Dedicated/Private deployments.
\Action items: see metadata section above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Moreno: ok, uh, thanks everyone for jumping on. we got about 75 minutes, we'll try to be efficient. quick intros?
[00:10] Priya Nair: hey, this is Priya, ML eng on Aurelia, we hit a regression after rolling AWQ on our summarization model, about 6-8% ROUGE drop on some prompt buckets.
[00:22] Marco Ruiz: Marco, infra, I was helping with the onprem deploy. we also saw intermittent latency spikes and a weird kv-cache miss rate in the logs.
[00:31] Samir Patel: thanks, yeah. Samir from Redwood, I looked at the sample traces you sent. first pass looked like layer 6-9 activations shifted when AWQ was enabled, so it matches a quantization-induced distribution shift hypothesis.
[00:45] Priya Nair: yeah, and it's odd because when we tried GPTQ deterministic quant it didn't regress as badly, but cost/latency hurt.
[00:55] Lina Cho: it's common, AWQ's stochastic rounding can change token probabilities on edge cases, but it should generally keep top-1 stable. the fact it's 6-8% suggests either layer-specific sensitivity or interaction with KV cache warmup.
[01:10] Tom Becker: quick business note — this is hitting a pilot with clinicians, timeline is tight, so we need a plan that minimizes user-visible noise.
[01:20] Marco Ruiz: also worth noting, our VPC had a short burst of packet drops during the rollout window; not sure if that correlated with retried requests and inconsistent KV states.
[01:34] Samir Patel: that's interesting — KV cache staleness can show up as semantic regressions if subsequent tokens rely on cached prefix states. sometimes reordering or retries can evict or rehydrate the cache in different states.
[01:47] Priya Nair: what exactly do you mean by 'rehydrate differently'? our traces show identical request IDs but different token probs across repeats.
[01:57] Samir Patel: a couple things: 1) if batching/coalescing merges requests across lanes, and AWQ introduces non-deterministic rounding, order of kernel execution can change floating rounding accumulation, 2) if the KV cache warmup path isn't idempotent or is missing a sticky key, retries can pick a slightly different cached chunk — small numeric diffs amplify in decoding loops.
[02:24] Dalia Wong: we did see a spike in coalesced batches during peak. we have autoscaling that increases batch size which may have changed scheduling.
[02:34] Alex Moreno: okay let's enumerate hypotheses: A) layerwise sensitivity to AWQ stochastic rounding, B) kv-cache warmup order & batch coalescing interactions, C) networking-induced replays creating divergent cache states, D) model compilation path selecting different kernels on specific sequence lengths.
[02:52] Priya Nair: we also tried fp8 in a canary and didn't see as bad a drop but code path was different — different kernels, so maybe kernel selection is a big factor.
[03:05] Samir Patel: right, FP8 uses different accumulation pathways and sometimes uses emulated fp8 routines on our runtime, which have different numeric profiles vs int8 AWQ. AWQ is known to be faster but more stochastic.
[03:20] Lina Cho: for reproduction we should run: deterministic GPTQ baseline, AWQ stochastic sweep (n=10 seeds), and FP8 run. keep identical batch ordering and disable coalescing to isolate. then reintroduce coalescing and KV warmup toggles.
[03:35] Tom Becker: can Redwood run those on our sample set? we can share the 100 failing prompts.
[03:40] Alex Moreno: yes we'll run it, Samir will own. deliverables: notebook + perf logs + top-20 diffs.
[03:50] 
[04:10] (screen-share noise/brief pause)
[04:28] Samir Patel: quick note on KV cache warmup: we have two priming strategies — prefix priming (replay the last n tokens) and sticky-kv (maintain KV shard affinity per session). in cloud-hosted mode sticky-kv is easier; in private deployments with multi-tenant GPUs we sometimes see shard remaps.
[04:50] Marco Ruiz: on our infra we're using fixed shard mapping but during scale events we observed reassignments that coincided with the rollout.
[05:00] Priya Nair: could remapping change which quantized kernel runs?
[05:06] Samir Patel: yes, because kernel selection looks at sequence length, hardware capabilities, and sometimes model shard placement. remap -> different execution graph -> different accumulation rounding order. it's subtle but real.
[05:24] Dalia Wong: ok, operationally how do we reduce user impact? do we fallback to GPTQ? or force FP8?
[05:33] Samir Patel: fallbacks are an option: Redwood runtime supports per-route precision fallback policies. canary -> if regression metric crosses threshold, route to GPTQ or to a model variant with deterministic quant. downside: higher latency/cost.
[05:45] Alex Moreno: there's also a middle ground: we can gate AWQ on batch size and disable coalescing for critical routes, plus implement a kv warmup sticky-affinity for those sessions. that reduces noise without full rollback.
[05:58] Priya Nair: that seems promising. how do we measure the warmup window? we saw regressions mostly for first seven tokens after context swap.
[06:10] Samir Patel: we measure per-token divergence across repeats. warmup window is often 5-15 tokens depending on model. we can instrument sticky kv hit rates and divergence score.
[06:22] Tom Becker: what's the perf hit if we disable coalescing on that route?
[06:27] Lina Cho: it depends on throughput. disabling coalescing increases p99 by about 10-30% in our benchmarks for low-latency routes but reduces batch-related variance. for a small pilot cohort it's acceptable.
[06:40] Marco Ruiz: noted. we can limit that to 5% of traffic initially.
[06:46] Samir Patel: another experiment: run AWQ with stochastic seeds fixed (deterministic AWQ run) — that mitigates randomness and keeps many benefits. it doesn't fully match GPTQ but gives a middle ground.
[06:58] Priya Nair: how reliably can you pin AWQ seeds in our onprem? we've seen random seed not honored in earlier rollout.
[07:06] Samir Patel: good call — that sounds like a bug in the runtime's seed propagation for private mode. we'll add a test case. Lina, can you own that?
[07:14] Lina Cho: yes, I'll add a deterministic AWQ verification test for both hosted and private modes.
[07:20] 
[07:35] (Background: keyboard, brief crosstalk)
[07:50] Priya Nair: one more oddity: some prompts only fail when KV cache is warm, others only fail cold — it's not uniform.
[07:59] Samir Patel: that suggests a non-linear interaction: for some prefixes, AWQ's rounding nudges probability mass away from the correct beam early, and cached tokens amplify the drift. we need token-level trace diffs.
[08:15] Dalia Wong: we can add token-prob dumps for the failing prompts, but that's heavy. what's the best minimal set?
[08:22] Samir Patel: top-k token probs for first 20 tokens and cumulative logprob diffs per token is usually enough. also include beam if used.
[08:35] Priya Nair: ok we'll provide those for the 100 prompts.
[08:40] 
[09:05] Alex Moreno: let's talk about deployment safety: recommended canary config — start with 2% traffic AWQ, deterministic seed, sticky kv warmup enabled, disable coalescing for those sessions, monitor divergence metric and customer KPIs for 72 hours.
[09:24] Marco Ruiz: does Redwood's console surface per-route token divergence?
[09:30] Samir Patel: we have an early-release metric in Redwood Console called 'quant divergence' that computes per-prompt KL and token diffs. we'll enable that on your account and add custom alerts.
[09:40] Tom Becker: good, we'll want a slack webhook for alerts.
[09:44] Samir Patel: can set up. also we'll export raw perf traces to your bucket for deeper analysis.
[09:52] 
[10:10] (brief pause)
[10:25] Marco Ruiz: networking question — the packet drops I mentioned earlier, could they cause a divergence we can't detect in logs?
[10:33] Samir Patel: yes, if retry semantics cause different ordering or duplicate application of prefix updates to the cache; also if partial prefix arrives and warmup path tries to use it. we recommend idempotent warmup: only mark warm when full prefix confirmed.
[10:51] Priya Nair: can Redwood change that behavior in our private plane?
[10:55] Samir Patel: yes, it's a runtime flag we can toggle per-deployment: 'kv_warm_mark_on_confirm'. we'll test it in the repro.
[11:05] Priya Nair: thanks.
[11:12] Alex Moreno: circling back to quant algorithms — quick primer for the group: GPTQ is layerwise, offline, deterministic quant with slower compile time but high fidelity; AWQ is faster, often online or lighter compile, but with stochastic rounding; FP8 gives a different dynamic range and sometimes better for activations but requires hardware/compile support.
[11:40] Tom Becker: for our clinicians, stability matters more than cost — maybe we go GPTQ for the route that feeds production.
[11:47] Lina Cho: great option. but cost increase likely 1.8x-2.5x tokens depending on model. alternative is hybrid: GPTQ for sensitive layers, AWQ for rest — we do layer gating.
[11:59] Priya Nair: can Redwood automate layer gating? like profile and gate the few top sensitive layers?
[12:05] Samir Patel: yes, Redwood Optimize has a layer-sensitivity profiler; we can run it against your sample set and produce a suggested gating map. we'll include that in the deliverables.
[12:15] Marco Ruiz: what's the expected time to run the profiler on our 100 prompts?
[12:19] Samir Patel: about 6-8 hours on a single GPU, less if parallelized. we'll queue it on a dedicated node.
[12:27] 
[12:40] Priya Nair: any known issues with FP8 & our current onprem A100s?
[12:45] Lina Cho: A100 supports TF32/FP16 natively; FP8 requires newer kernels or emulation; runtime will emulate FP8 which adds some overhead. the numeric profile can be better for certain activations but it's workload dependent.
[12:57] Dalia Wong: sounds like FP8 maybe not worth it if we already saw FP8 canary ok but slow.
[13:03] Samir Patel: it's an option for experiments, not primary.
[13:08] 
[13:25] Alex Moreno: testing plan recap: 1) Customer provides 100 failing prompts + top-k token traces, 2) Redwood runs gated repro: GPTQ baseline, AWQ deterministic seeds (n=3), AWQ stochastic sweep (n=10), FP8 run — all with coalescing on/off and kv warmup toggles, 3) Layer-sensitivity profiler and suggested layer gating, 4) Onprem 2-hour profiling session.
[13:55] Priya Nair: timeline ok. we'll send prompts by Friday.
[14:02] Marco Ruiz: I'll open the VPC peering and share configs; expect some firewall rules.
[14:07] Samir Patel: we'll need SSH host + bench bucket and minimal SA.
[14:12] Priya Nair: security question: can Redwood sign an additional DPA addendum for the onprem bench?
[14:18] Alex Moreno: yes, our legal team has a template. I'll send it, expect a 2-3 day turnaround.
[14:22] Tom Becker: last Q: if we identify a single offending layer, how fast can you push a gated prod change?
[14:29] Samir Patel: with a rollout policy and canary, we can push within a day, assuming model artifacts are already compiled. if we need a new quant compile, add ~4-12 hours.
[14:40] Dalia Wong: great.
[14:45] Alex Moreno: ok let's capture action items and wrap. thanks everyone. we'll send the notebook links + console enablement and schedule the bench.
[14:55] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard product names (e.g., "Redwood Dedi" for Dedicated), speaker overlaps, and token/prob nomenclature simplified.
